answer.observations: Baseline E0 shows UDP delivering 979 Mbps with 51.0% loss and 911591 sender-side drops, while TCP goodput is 0 bps with 3 retransmissions and reverse-link utilization is 0.0.

whys.result: tcp_goodput_bps=0, tcp_retrans=3, l1_util_back=0.0, udp_loss_frac=0.510489, l1_drops=911591.
whys.guess: UDP fills the sender-side FIFO queue, so TCP SYN/data packets are tail-dropped before reaching the receiver; no SYN-ACK or data ACKs are produced, and the 3 retransmissions are TCP retries that never establish delivery.

whys.result: tcp_goodput_bps=0 with only tcp_retrans=3 under TcpCubic.
whys.guess: TcpCubic's loss/RTO response makes the TCP sender stop after a few retries; a different TCP congestion control could deliver data despite the same FIFO queue.

whys.result: tcp_goodput_bps=0 with l1.queue.length=100 and heavy UDP loss.
whys.guess: The queue length 100 is too short to admit TCP packets before UDP fills it; a much longer FIFO queue would let TCP handshake and deliver some data.

hypotheses.text: Replacing the sender-side FIFO queue with a scheduler queue will let TCP reach the receiver and deliver data, so tcp_goodput_bps becomes greater than 0.
Changing tcp.type to TcpBbr while keeping the FIFO queue will let TCP reach the receiver and deliver data, so tcp_goodput_bps becomes greater than 0.
Increasing l1.queue.length to 1000 while keeping TcpCubic and the FIFO queue will let TCP reach the receiver and deliver data, so tcp_goodput_bps becomes greater than 0.

answer.observations: E1 shows scheduler r002 delivers 482007923 bps TCP and 489526240 bps UDP, q1000 r004 only 5792 bps TCP, and Bbr r003 remains 0 bps; I request probes of r002, r003, and r004 to inspect TCP state and scheduler service.

whys.result: r002 with the sender-side scheduler measured tcp_goodput_bps=482007923 and udp_goodput_bps=489526240, with l1_util_back=0.009208 and tcp_retrans=71.
whys.guess: The scheduler queue gives UDP and TCP roughly equal service on l1, so TCP can establish and its goodput is capped near half the 1Gbps link rather than by the FIFO queue length.

whys.result: r004 with l1.queue.length=1000 measured tcp_goodput_bps=5792, tcp_retrans=18, and l1_util_back=0.0.
whys.guess: A 1000-packet FIFO still lets UDP monopolize the link; TCP only slips through during rare queue gaps and loses most ACKs, so it remains in RTO/probe state and delivers only a few bytes.

whys.result: r003 with TcpBbr measured tcp_goodput_bps=0 and tcp_retrans=3, identical to r001.
whys.guess: Under the FIFO queue TCP never receives ACKs, so the congestion-control algorithm is not engaged beyond initial retries; BBR cannot change the outcome.

whys.result: r002 scheduler measured tcp_goodput_bps=482007923 with tcp_retrans=71 and l1_drops_tcp=71.
whys.guess: Increasing the scheduler queue length to 1000 will reduce TCP queue drops/retransmissions and raise tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1%.

whys.result: r002 scheduler established TCP (tcp_goodput_bps=482007923) while r003 BBR under FIFO did not.
whys.guess: Under a scheduler, TcpBbr's bandwidth probing will capture more than TcpCubic's fair share and raise tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1%.

hypotheses.text: With the sender-side scheduler, increasing l1.queue.length from 100 to 1000 will not change tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1% relative to the scheduler TcpCubic run.
With the sender-side scheduler, changing tcp.type to TcpBbr will not change tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1% relative to the scheduler TcpCubic run.

answer.observations: E2 shows scheduler q1000 (r005) gives tcp_goodput_bps=476482765 with tcp_retrans=0, and scheduler BBR (r006) gives tcp_goodput_bps=190096915 while udp_goodput_bps=785971200. I request probes of r005/r006 and test scheduler q4, q250, and TcpBic against scheduler Cubic q100.

whys.result: r005 scheduler q1000 measured tcp_goodput_bps=476482765 with tcp_retrans=0 and l1_drops_tcp=0, 1.15% below r002's 482007923 bps.
whys.guess: The scheduler caps each flow near its class share, so a longer queue mainly adds delay and slightly lowers Cubic's rate even though it removes TCP drops.

whys.result: r006 scheduler BBR measured tcp_goodput_bps=190096915 and udp_goodput_bps=785971200, while r002 Cubic measured tcp_goodput_bps=482007923 and udp_goodput_bps=489526240.
whys.guess: BBR paces below its scheduler class share, leaving spare scheduler capacity to UDP; loss-based TCP that fills its class gets the fair share.

whys.result: Changing scheduler queue length from 100 to 1000 changed TCP goodput by only 1.15% and removed all TCP drops.
whys.guess: Queue delay, not TCP drops, limits scheduler TCP; a 4-packet or 250-packet queue would reduce delay enough to raise tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1% over q100.

whys.result: BBR under scheduler is far below Cubic, while Cubic is near the scheduler payload share.
whys.guess: TcpBic under scheduler can exceed TcpCubic by more than 1% by filling or probing the scheduler class better.

hypotheses.text: With the sender-side scheduler and TcpCubic, l1.queue.length=4 or 250 will not raise tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1% over l1.queue.length=100.
With the sender-side scheduler and l1.queue.length=100, TcpBic will not raise tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1% over TcpCubic.

answer.observations: E3 shows scheduler q250 and TcpBic match r002 at 482007923/482131872 bps within tolerance, while q4 is 463881280 bps with 3417 retransmissions. I request measures/probes for r003-r009 and test CoDel/FQ-CoDel against the scheduler.

whys.result: Scheduler q250 and Bic match q100 Cubic (482007923, 482131872 bps) while q4 is 463881280 bps and BBR is 190096915 bps.
whys.guess: The sender-side scheduler gives TCP a guaranteed class share near 482 Mbps; queue length and loss-based TCP type only change drops, not this cap.

whys.result: All best scheduler runs are near 482 Mbps, but no alternative queue disc has been tested.
whys.guess: CoDel or FQ-CoDel could raise TCP above the scheduler by dropping UDP more aggressively or giving lower-delay fair service.

whys.result: Scheduler q4 measured 463881280 bps with tcp_retrans=3417 and l1_drops_tcp=3416.
whys.guess: A 4-packet scheduler queue is too short for TCP's class, so TCP packets are dropped and throughput falls.

whys.result: Scheduler TcpBic measured 482131872 bps with tcp_retrans=1901, equal to Cubic within tolerance.
whys.guess: TcpBic fills the same scheduler class share as Cubic; its extra retransmissions do not lower average delivered goodput.

hypotheses.text: With l1.queue.length=100 and TcpCubic, replacing the sender-side scheduler with CoDel or FQ-CoDel will not raise tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1% over the scheduler run r002.

answer.observations: E4 shows CoDel r010 has tcp_goodput_bps=0 and l1_util_back=0.0, while FQ-CoDel r011 has tcp_goodput_bps=482007923 with reverse traffic; FQ-CoDel also has tcp_retrans=6100 versus scheduler r002's 71 at identical TCP goodput.

whys.result: CoDel r010 measured tcp_goodput_bps=0, l1_util_back=0.0, l1_drops=911591, while FQ-CoDel r011 measured tcp_goodput_bps=482007923 and l1_util_back=0.009398.
whys.guess: CoDel is a single queue without per-flow isolation, so under 2Gbps UDP it drops TCP like FIFO; FQ-CoDel separates flows and gives TCP service.

whys.result: CoDel q100 starves TCP while FQ-CoDel q100 delivers 482007923 bps.
whys.guess: CoDel starvation is caused by l1.queue.length=100 being too short; a 1000-packet CoDel queue would let TCP packets survive and deliver data.

whys.result: FQ-CoDel r011 measured tcp_goodput_bps=482007923 and tcp_retrans=6100, while scheduler r002 measured the same goodput and tcp_retrans=71; total l1_drops differ by 6028, close to the retransmission difference 6029.
whys.guess: FQ-CoDel drops TCP more often and adds delay, so TCP keeps more bytes in flight to maintain the same fair share; the extra retransmissions are lost TCP segments, not a larger class share.

whys.result: FQ-CoDel and scheduler have identical TCP goodput but FQ-CoDel has 6100 retransmissions versus 71.
whys.guess: The extra retransmissions are spurious duplicates or artifacts that do not reflect extra TCP drops or a larger TCP window; TCP state is unchanged.

hypotheses.text: With CoDel and l1.queue.length=1000, tcp_goodput_bps remains below 1,000,000 bps.
With FQ-CoDel, mean tcp_inflight is more than 1% larger than with the scheduler at the same knobs.

answer.observations: E5/C9/V9 show CoDel q1000 r012 still starves TCP (1158 bps, 7 retrans) versus CoDel q100 r010 (0 bps, 3 retrans). H10 remains open and F11 has not yet been inspected, so I request r012 probe/series plus readings for F10/F2/F8 and repair the FQ-CoDel inflight test on existing runs.

whys.result: CoDel q1000 r012 measured tcp_goodput_bps=1158 and tcp_retrans=7, while CoDel q100 r010 measured tcp_goodput_bps=0 and tcp_retrans=3.
whys.guess: The larger CoDel queue lets a few TCP probe or retransmitted packets survive, but CoDel still has no per-flow isolation, so TCP never gets sustained ACKs and remains starved.

hypotheses.text: With FQ-CoDel and l1.queue.length=100, TcpCubic, mean tcp_inflight is within 1% of the scheduler run at the same knobs.

drop.why: H10 predicted larger inflight, which is not a consequence of Y20; H11 states the testable consequence of Y20 that TCP state is unchanged.

answer.observations: E6/C10/V10 show H11 was inconclusive because the one-sided inflight rule HELD at 72362.352 versus 136959.08; T21/T22 show FQ-CoDel has lower inflight and about half the RTT of the scheduler at identical TCP goodput. I request queue-wait/cwnd/CoDel inflight readings and test the inflight/RTT ratio on existing runs.

whys.result: r011 fqcodel tcp_rtt_ms mean=1.049359 ms versus r002 scheduler tcp_rtt_ms mean=2.092923 ms at tcp_goodput_bps=482007923.
whys.guess: FQ-CoDel's CoDel queue keeps the sender-side queueing delay lower than the scheduler TCP class queue, so the measured RTT is about half.

whys.result: r011 fqcodel tcp_inflight_mean=72362.352 and tcp_rtt_ms=1.049359 versus r002 scheduler tcp_inflight_mean=136959.08 and tcp_rtt_ms=2.092923 at identical tcp_goodput_bps=482007923.
whys.guess: Mean bytes in flight track delivered rate times RTT, so the lower FQ-CoDel RTT from shorter queueing explains its lower inflight rather than a different TCP share.

whys.result: The same FQ-CoDel/scheduler records show lower inflight and lower RTT; if the lower inflight were a smaller TCP window independent of RTT, mean(tcp_inflight/tcp_rtt_ms) would differ by more than 10%.
whys.guess: The lower FQ-CoDel inflight is caused by a smaller TCP congestion window/share independent of RTT, not by the lower RTT.

hypotheses.text: With FQ-CoDel and scheduler at l1.queue.length=100 and TcpCubic, mean(tcp_inflight/tcp_rtt_ms) for FQ-CoDel is within 10% of the scheduler value.

decisions.reason: CoDel runs have no reverse ACK traffic and near-zero TCP delivery even at q1000, while FQ-CoDel restores reverse ACKs and the scheduler-like TCP share, showing per-flow isolation rather than queue length explains the split.
Testing whether inflight/RTT is the same in FQ-CoDel and scheduler will show whether lower inflight follows from lower RTT.
Queue-wait readings for r011 and r002 will test whether FQ-CoDel's lower RTT comes from shorter sender queueing.

answer.observations: E7/C11/V11 show FQ-CoDel and scheduler inflight/RTT ratios differ by 6.8%, and T25/T26 show FQ-CoDel queue wait is lower; T29/T30 show CoDel q1000 had a brief 94120-byte inflight burst versus 1448 at q100. I close F10 and F11 and report the best settings.

decisions.reason: Identical goodput is explained by lower FQ-CoDel RTT and inflight, and the 6100-versus-71 retransmission gap matches the 6028 extra total drops in E4/E6.
The larger CoDel queue only lets a few TCP probe or retransmitted packets survive, as shown by the brief 94120-byte inflight burst and tiny measured goodput.

report.limit: At this recommendation the 1Gbps link is saturated and the locked UDP flow offers 2Gbps; the sender-side scheduler gives each flow a part of the link, so TCP is capped near half the link at 482007923 bps, and the tested queue lengths and TCP types stay at or below that share (E1,E2,E3,E4,E6,E7,C1,C4,C5,C6,C7,C8,V1,V4,V5,V6,V7,V8).
report.explanation: With the default FIFO or plain CoDel, UDP fills the sender queue and TCP never gets sustained ACKs, giving 0 bps (E0,E4,E5). Replacing the sender queue with a scheduler or FQ-CoDel isolates flows, lets TCP establish, and yields about 482 Mbps (E1,E4). The scheduler/FQ-CoDel service then caps TCP near its fair share: q250 and TcpBic match q100 Cubic within tolerance, q4 and q1000 are lower, and BBR is much lower (E2,E3). FQ-CoDel reaches the same goodput with lower RTT and inflight, and its extra retransmissions match the extra total drops, while CoDel q1000 only lets a few TCP probes survive (E4,E5,E6,E7,T20,T21,T22,T25,T26,T29,T30,C11,V11). Scheduler q100 Cubic is preferred because it ties the maximum observed TCP goodput with fewer retransmissions than FQ-CoDel or Bic and a shorter queue than q250; expected values are tcp_goodput_bps=482007923, udp_goodput_bps=489526240, and tcp_retrans=71.

claims.text: Per-flow isolation is required for TCP to deliver data under the locked 2Gbps UDP flow.
The best TCP goodput observed is 482007923 bps with scheduler or FQ-CoDel at l1.queue.length=100 and TcpCubic.
Queue length and loss-based TCP type do not raise scheduler TCP goodput beyond 1%: q250 and TcpBic match q100 Cubic, while q4, q1000, and BBR do not exceed it.
The cap is fair service on the saturated link: UDP and TCP each receive about half the 1Gbps link, and FQ-CoDel's lower inflight tracks its lower RTT at identical TCP goodput.
FQ-CoDel's 6100 retransmissions versus scheduler's 71 at identical goodput are explained by extra TCP drops, not a larger TCP share; CoDel q1000's small 1158 bps is only occasional probe survival.
